answers.text: Advertising must be tailored to each medium for maximum reach across diverse audience demographics worldwide.
answers.feedback: A marketing tactic, not McLuhan's thesis. See Week 01: Introduction to Persuasion — The Medium is the Message.

answers.text: The form of a medium reshapes perception more than the content it carries.
answers.feedback: Correct. See Week 01: Introduction to Persuasion — McLuhan, The Medium is the Message.

answers.text: A strong message can succeed independently of the medium chosen to deliver it to the target audience.
answers.feedback: Opposite of McLuhan. Review Week 01: Introduction to Persuasion.

answers.text: Television replaces print as the dominant medium of public discourse in the second half of the twentieth century.
answers.feedback: Related but not the meaning of the phrase. See Week 01: Introduction to Persuasion — McLuhan reading.

questions.name: McLuhan — medium and message
questions.question: Recall the McLuhan reading discussed in class. "The medium is the message" most directly argues that:

answers.text: Story.
answers.feedback: Story is #2 (23%). Review Week 08: Post-Production Polish — Murch hierarchy.

answers.text: Rhythm.
answers.feedback: Rhythm is #3 (10%). Review Week 08: Post-Production Polish — Murch hierarchy.

answers.text: Emotion.
answers.feedback: Correct — emotion at 51%. See Week 08: Post-Production Polish — Murch Rule of Six (51% priority).

answers.text: 3D continuity of action across the frame.
answers.feedback: 3D continuity is at the bottom of the hierarchy (4%). See Week 08: Post-Production Polish — Murch Rule of Six.

questions.name: Murch — Rule of Six top priority
questions.question: From the post-production class on Walter Murch's Rule of Six, the highest priority when choosing where to cut is:

answers.text: Long takes preserve emotional truth more faithfully than rapidly intercut shot/reverse-shot sequences.
answers.feedback: A separate aesthetic argument, not Kuleshov. See Week 04: Soviet Montage & Kuleshov Effect.

answers.text: Stanislavski-trained actors produce more legible micro-expressions than untrained performers do on camera.
answers.feedback: Acting theory, not the Kuleshov experiment. Review Week 04: Soviet Montage & Kuleshov.

answers.text: A face's meaning is shaped by the shot that follows it.
answers.feedback: Correct — meaning is constructed by editing context. See Week 04: Soviet Montage & Kuleshov Effect.

answers.text: Black-and-white footage carries stronger emotional weight than colour footage for early-cinema audiences.
answers.feedback: Not a Kuleshov claim. Review Week 04: Soviet Montage & Kuleshov Effect.

questions.name: Kuleshov effect
questions.question: The Kuleshov effect demonstrates that:

answers.text: A sound whose source is heard but not yet seen on screen.
answers.feedback: Correct. Chion uses "acousmatic" for sound separated from a visible source. See Week 11: Audio Mixing for Advertisement — Chion and acousmatic sound.

answers.text: A sound that is recorded without compression so that its waveform remains mathematically lossless.
answers.feedback: That describes a technical audio format issue, not Chion''s film-sound concept. Review Week 11: Audio Mixing — Chion and film-sound vocabulary.

answers.text: A sound effect synchronized exactly to a visible movement so the cut feels seamless.
answers.feedback: This confuses acousmatic sound with synchronization. See Week 11: Audio Mixing — diegetic, non-diegetic, and Chion vocabulary.

answers.text: A musical cue that exists outside the story world and can only be heard by the audience.
answers.feedback: That is non-diegetic sound. Acousmatic sound is defined by whether the source is visible, not simply by story-world status.

questions.name: Chion — acousmatic sound
questions.question: In Michel Chion's vocabulary, an acousmatic sound is:

answers.text: Cutting on motion to preserve the spatial continuity of the action across the cut.
answers.feedback: Continuity editing — what Eisenstein contested. See Week 04: Soviet Montage & Kuleshov Effect — Eisenstein montage types.

answers.text: Alternating shot lengths rapidly to drive the emotional rhythm of the sequence forward across the climax.
answers.feedback: Closer to rhythmic montage, a different category. Review Week 04: Soviet Montage — Eisenstein typology.

answers.text: Synchronizing visual cuts to musical beats sourced from the orchestral score of the film itself.
answers.feedback: Tonal montage relates to mood/key, not literal beat-sync. See Week 04: Soviet Montage — Eisenstein montage categories.

answers.text: Juxtaposing two shots to generate a concept that exists in neither shot alone.
answers.feedback: Correct — dialectical synthesis. See Week 04: Soviet Montage & Kuleshov Effect — Intellectual montage.

questions.name: Eisenstein — intellectual montage
questions.question: Eisenstein's "intellectual montage" produces meaning by:

answers.text: A jump cut, eliding part of the action in a temporally jarring way for stylistic effect on screen.
answers.feedback: Jump cuts are about temporal elision, not the spatial axis. Review Week 03: Continuity & Gestalt — 180° rule.

answers.text: Apparent reversal of screen direction, disorienting the viewer.
answers.feedback: Correct. See Week 03: Continuity & Gestalt — 180° rule violation consequences.

answers.text: A match-on-action that maintains continuity through the kinetic momentum of on-screen movement itself.
answers.feedback: Match-on-action is unrelated to the 180° axis. See Week 03: Continuity & Gestalt — match cuts and axis.

answers.text: A graphic match exploiting the visual similarity between two shapes from different times and places.
answers.feedback: Graphic match is about composition, not the axis line. Review Week 03: Continuity & Gestalt.

questions.name: 180-degree rule
questions.question: Crossing the 180° axis between two consecutive shots most commonly produces:

answers.text: True
answers.feedback: Correct. See Week 05: Breaking Rules & Experimental — Godard and the jump cut.

answers.text: False
answers.feedback: It is true. Review Week 05: Breaking Rules & Experimental — Nouvelle Vague techniques.

questions.name: Jump cut origin
questions.question: The jump cut became a defining stylistic device of the Nouvelle Vague, popularised by Godard's Breathless (1960).

answers.text: Mark a temporal ellipsis by overlapping two simultaneous events into one continuous spatial frame for the viewer.
answers.feedback: Describes split-screen, not an L-cut. See Week 03: Continuity & Gestalt — split edits and L-cuts.

answers.text: Insert a cutaway shot between two pieces of dialogue while maintaining the same shot scale on both speakers.
answers.feedback: Generic cutaway — does not require an L-cut. Review Week 03: Continuity & Gestalt — J-cuts and L-cuts.

answers.text: Carry audio from the outgoing shot under the incoming picture.
answers.feedback: Correct — smooths the transition. See Week 03: Continuity & Gestalt — split edits (J-cuts and L-cuts).

answers.text: Trim a clip's in-point and out-point simultaneously by a fixed number of frames using the slip-edit tool.
answers.feedback: That is a slip edit. Review Week 03: Continuity & Gestalt — trim vs slip vs slide edits.

questions.name: L-cut / split edit
questions.question: An L-cut (split edit) is most commonly used to:

answers.text: Captions are always burned in (open) and motion graphics are always sidecar files attached to the export container of the deliverable.
answers.feedback: Both can be open or sidecar. See Week 08: Post-Production Polish — Captions vs motion graphics.

answers.text: Captions and motion graphics are now governed by the unified CEA-708 broadcast standard for digital deliverables across all major platforms.
answers.feedback: Honeypot — CEA-708 covers closed captions only. Review Week 08: Post-Production Polish — caption standards.

answers.text: Captions transliterate spoken audio for accessibility; motion graphics are designed visual elements.
answers.feedback: Correct. See Week 08: Post-Production Polish — captions vs motion graphics distinction.

answers.text: Motion graphics are exported in SRT or VTT sidecar files while captions are baked into .mogrt template format inside Adobe ecosystems.
answers.feedback: Inverted definitions. Review Week 08: Post-Production Polish — captions and subtitles.

questions.name: Captions vs motion graphics
questions.question: Which statement most precisely captures the distinction between captions and motion-graphics text?

answers.text: After the creative grade so that aesthetic choices remain visible across all tonal regions of the image throughout the edit.
answers.feedback: Inverted workflow. See Week 08: Post-Production Polish — Lumetri Color workflow (primary before creative).

answers.text: Only on Log footage, since Rec.709 footage is already neutralized at the camera and does not require correction.
answers.feedback: Both Log and Rec.709 typically benefit from correction. Review Week 08: Post-Production Polish — color correction fundamentals.

answers.text: Before any creative grade or LUT.
answers.feedback: Correct — neutralize first, stylize second. See Week 08: Post-Production Polish — Lumetri Color panel workflow.

answers.text: Exclusively in the export stage via the Adobe Media Encoder so as not to overwrite raw camera metadata.
answers.feedback: Color is corrected in the timeline, not at export. Review Week 08: Post-Production Polish — color workflow.

questions.name: Lumetri — primary correction order
questions.question: In the Lumetri Color exercise from class, primary correction is performed:

answers.text: −23 dB — the EBU R128 broadcast standard adopted across European public-broadcasting organisations.
answers.feedback: EBU R128 is a broadcast loudness standard, not a peak level target. See Week 11: Audio Mixing for Advertisement — peak levels and normalization.

answers.text: −6 dB, leaving more headroom than most social/streaming masters need for normal delivery.
answers.feedback: Too conservative for this course target — it can waste dynamic range without additional benefit for most platforms. Review Week 11: Audio Mixing — optimal headroom for streaming.

answers.text: −3 to −4 dB.
answers.feedback: Correct. Leaves safe headroom below 0 dBFS while preserving useful dynamic range. See Week 11: Audio Mixing for Advertisement — export targets.

answers.text: 0 dB, since digital audio is calibrated relative to full scale and any negative value indicates a quieter master.
answers.feedback: 0 dBFS is full scale and would clip. Review Week 11: Audio Mixing — digital audio fundamentals.

questions.name: Peak level for streaming
questions.question: A safe peak level target for streaming delivery (YouTube, social) to leave headroom and avoid platform normalization crushing your mix is approximately:

answers.text: A container compresses video data while a codec organises the resulting bitstream into a single file with metadata for playback.
answers.feedback: Inverted. See Week 08: Post-Production Polish — containers vs codecs.

answers.text: A codec is the wrapper that bundles audio and video tracks while the container is the encoder responsible for compression efficiency.
answers.feedback: Inverted definitions. Review Week 08: Post-Production Polish — export formats.

answers.text: A container is a wrapper format; a codec is the algorithm that encodes the streams.
answers.feedback: Correct. MP4/MOV/MKV = containers; H.264/H.265/ProRes = codecs. See Week 08: Post-Production Polish — export specifications table.

answers.text: Containers and codecs are interchangeable; the technical literature distinguishes them mostly for legacy reasons inherited from broadcast workflows.
answers.feedback: They are not interchangeable. See Week 08: Post-Production Polish — containers vs codecs.

questions.name: Container vs codec
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a container from a codec?

answers.text: A codec, derived from the MPEG-4 family of compression standards developed by the Moving Picture Experts Group during the 1990s.
answers.feedback: Honeypot — common confusion. MP4 is a container, not a codec. See Week 08: Post-Production Polish — export specifications table.

answers.text: A delivery profile defined by ISO/IEC for streaming over adaptive HTTP-based protocols in modern OTT distribution chains.
answers.feedback: Plausible-sounding but incorrect. Review Week 08: Post-Production Polish — export formats overview.

answers.text: A container format.
answers.feedback: Correct — MPEG-4 Part 14 container; can hold H.264, H.265, AAC, etc. See Week 08: Post-Production Polish — export specifications table.

answers.text: A proprietary Apple format originally designed for QuickTime that was later adopted as a generic web video standard.
answers.feedback: MP4 is an open ISO standard; QuickTime .mov is the Apple format. Review Week 08: Post-Production Polish — containers vs codecs.

questions.name: MP4 — what is it?
questions.question: MP4 (.mp4) is best classified as:

answers.text: Scale the original up by approximately 178% so the 1080-pixel height fills the 1920-pixel target frame entirely without any background fill.
answers.feedback: Forces a 178% upscale on the main image. See Week 07: Production Sprint – Team Videothon — reframing strategies.

answers.text: Apply Premiere's Auto Reframe with the slowest motion-tracking preset to follow subject motion across all shots in the timeline.
answers.feedback: Auto Reframe still upscales 1080-height source. Review Week 08: Post-Production Polish — Auto Reframe limitations.

answers.text: Keep the main subject at native scale, center/crop it as needed, and fill the vertical frame with a blurred copy.
answers.feedback: Correct — the subject stays 1:1 with no upscaling; the blurred layer fills the empty vertical space. See Week 07: Production Sprint – Team Videothon — reframing strategies.

answers.text: Export at 1920×1080 with a 9:16 metadata flag attached to the container and let the platform crop the frame on playback.
answers.feedback: Platforms ignore such metadata. Review Week 09: Digital Platforms, Algorithms & Ethics — platform specifications.

questions.name: Reframing horizontal to vertical
questions.question: Your master is 1920×1080 (16:9). For TikTok delivery (1080×1920) with the original at 1080p (not 4K), which strategy preserves the most fidelity on the main subject?

answers.text: The video essay is always narrated by an off-screen voice while video art relies exclusively on diegetic ambient sound captured during recording.
answers.feedback: Both can use any sound strategy. See Video Essay Monograph — sound design in video essays.

answers.text: Video essays are distributed online while video art is always installed inside galleries and museums for in-person viewing only.
answers.feedback: Distribution channels overlap. Review Video Art Monograph — exhibition contexts and online distribution.

answers.text: The video essay develops an argument; video art foregrounds the medium itself.
answers.feedback: Correct — argument vs. material/formal investigation. See Video Essay Monograph and Video Art Monograph — form distinctions.

answers.text: Video art uses experimental editing whereas the video essay is restricted to classical continuity grammar inherited from Hollywood narrative cinema.
answers.feedback: Video essays freely use experimental techniques. Review Video Essay Monograph — stylistic approaches.

questions.name: Video essay vs video art
questions.question: Which difference most fundamentally separates the video essay from video art?

answers.text: The total volume of advertising and televised content circulating across mass-media channels in late capitalism.
answers.feedback: Common misreading — Debord defines spectacle as a social relation, not a quantity of media. See Week 01: Introduction to Persuasion — Debord and the spectacle.

answers.text: A communication strategy used by the ruling class to consolidate political power through staged public events worldwide.
answers.feedback: Closer to a Marxist propaganda critique; Debord's concept is broader. Review Week 01: Introduction to Persuasion — Debord reading.

answers.text: A social relation between people, mediated by images.
answers.feedback: Correct — Debord's thesis #4. See Week 01: Introduction to Persuasion — Society of the Spectacle.

answers.text: The subjective experience of being overwhelmed by visual stimuli in modern urban environments and screens.
answers.feedback: Phenomenological reading; not Debord's definition. Review Week 01: Introduction to Persuasion — Debord's Society of the Spectacle.

questions.name: Debord — the spectacle
questions.question: For Guy Debord, "the spectacle" is best understood as:

answers.text: Reproduce the perceptual habits of theatre-trained spectators within the framework of a fully cinematic medium.
answers.feedback: Vertov rejected theatrical fiction. See Week 04: Soviet Montage & Kuleshov Effect — Vertov and kino-eye.

answers.text: Use the camera and montage to reveal truths invisible to the human eye.
answers.feedback: Correct. See Week 04: Soviet Montage & Kuleshov Effect — Vertov and the camera as truth-revealer.

answers.text: Build a documentary aesthetic grounded in observational long takes captured by static cameras inside factories during work shifts.
answers.feedback: Honeypot — confuses Vertov with later Direct Cinema. Review Week 04: Soviet Montage — Vertov montage vs observational documentary.

answers.text: Train audiences to read intertitles as the primary bearer of meaning across silent-era propaganda films of the period.
answers.feedback: Vertov resisted intertitles in favour of visual montage. See Week 04: Soviet Montage & Kuleshov Effect — Vertov montage aesthetics.

questions.name: Vertov — kino-eye
questions.question: Vertov's kino-eye programme aimed to:

answers.text: 2 Mbps, corresponding to the platform's baseline profile for low-bandwidth viewers on mobile networks worldwide.
answers.feedback: Too low. See Week 09: Digital Platforms, Algorithms & Ethics — YouTube recommended bitrates.

answers.text: 8 Mbps.
answers.feedback: Correct per official YouTube guidance. See Week 09: Digital Platforms, Algorithms & Ethics — platform specs and bitrate recommendations.

answers.text: 50 Mbps, in line with archival mezzanine recommendations published in YouTube's creator-academy advanced workflow notes.
answers.feedback: Closer to mastering bitrates. Review Week 09: Digital Platforms, Algorithms & Ethics — mezzanine vs delivery bitrates.

answers.text: 100 Mbps, matching the bitrate ceiling YouTube imposes per resolution tier across all uploads from verified creators.
answers.feedback: Far above recommendation. See Week 09: Digital Platforms, Algorithms & Ethics — bitrate ceilings and diminishing returns.

questions.name: YouTube 1080p bitrate
questions.question: YouTube's recommended H.264 upload bitrate for SDR 1080p (24–30 fps) is approximately:

answers.text: True
answers.feedback: Incorrect — Instagram does not support 4K Reels; downscale to 1080×1920 before upload. See Week 09: Digital Platforms, Algorithms & Ethics — Instagram specs.

answers.text: False
answers.feedback: Correct — pre-downscale to 1080p. See Week 09: Digital Platforms, Algorithms & Ethics — Instagram Reels specifications.

questions.name: Instagram supports 4K Reels
questions.question: Instagram Reels currently supports 4K vertical (2160×3840) uploads natively.

answers.text: A French Nouvelle Vague filmmaker known for radical jump-cut grammar in the early 1960s feature-film output.
answers.feedback: Godard et al., not Paik. Review Video Art Monograph — Nam June Paik biography.

answers.text: A pioneer of video art.
answers.feedback: Correct. See Video Art Monograph — Nam June Paik and video art origins.

answers.text: A Soviet montage theorist active in the 1920s alongside Eisenstein, Vertov and Kuleshov within the early film-school institutions.
answers.feedback: Wrong era. Review Video Art Monograph — Nam June Paik timeline (1960s-2000s).

answers.text: A documentary director of observational television series for the BBC during the post-war public-broadcasting expansion.
answers.feedback: Unrelated. See Video Art Monograph — Nam June Paik vs documentary traditions.

questions.question: Nam June Paik is most often credited as:
